tool.name: Plotly
tool.tagline: Interactive, web-ready charts in Python with Plotly Express and graph objects
tool.description: Plotly is a Python graphing library that produces interactive charts rendered by the plotly.js JavaScript engine: hover tooltips, zoom, pan and legend toggling work out of the box in notebooks, HTML files and web apps. Plotly Express builds most charts from a DataFrame in one line, while graph objects give full control over every trace and layout property.

concepts.name: The figure: data, layout and plotly.js
concepts.summary: Every Plotly chart is a figure made of a list of traces (data) and a layout, serialized to JSON and drawn by plotly.js.
concepts.why: Knowing that a figure is just structured data explains how every update, export and integration works.
concepts.body:
A Plotly **figure** is a tree of attributes with two main branches:

- `data`: a list of **traces**. Each trace is one series of a given type, such as `scatter`, `bar`, `histogram` or `heatmap`, with its own `x`, `y`, `marker`, `name` and so on.
- `layout`: everything that is not data: title, axes (`xaxis`, `yaxis`), legend, margins, size, template, annotations and shapes.

(A third branch, `frames`, holds animation frames.)

In Python the figure is a `plotly.graph_objects.Figure` object, which validates every attribute: misspell `marker.colour` and you get an error listing valid names instead of a silently ignored setting. `fig.to_dict()` and `fig.to_json()` show the raw structure, and `print(fig)` displays it compactly.

Rendering does not happen in Python at all. The figure is serialized to JSON and handed to **plotly.js**, a JavaScript library, in a notebook, a browser tab or an HTML file. That is why Plotly charts are interactive by default: hover tooltips, box zoom, pan, double-click to reset, and clicking legend entries to hide traces.

There are two ways to build figures:

- **Plotly Express** (`import plotly.express as px`): one function call per chart from a DataFrame, returning a ready-made figure.
- **Graph objects** (`import plotly.graph_objects as go`): construct traces and layout yourself for full control.

Both produce the same `Figure` class, so you can start with Express and refine with graph-object methods.
concepts.code:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(
    data=[go.Bar(x=["a", "b", "c"], y=[3, 1, 2], name="sales")],
    layout=go.Layout(title=dict(text="Sales by product")),
)
d = fig.to_dict()
print(list(d))                          # ['data', 'layout']
print(d["data"][0]["type"])             # bar
print(fig.layout.title.text)            # Sales by product

try:
    go.Bar(marker=dict(colour="red"))   # typo is caught
except ValueError as e:
    print(str(e).splitlines()[2])       # Did you mean "color"?
fig.write_html("sales.html")            # open in a browser: fully interactive
takeaways: A figure = list of traces (`data`) + `layout` (+ optional `frames`)
plotly.js renders the JSON in the browser, which makes charts interactive
Graph objects validate attribute names and values
pitfalls: Expecting matplotlib-style rendering in Python; output always needs a browser-like environment or an export step.

quiz.q: Where does a title belong in a Plotly figure?
quiz.explain: Anything not tied to one series, such as titles, axes and legend, lives in the layout.

concepts.name: Plotly Express: charts from a DataFrame
concepts.summary: Create scatter, line and bar charts with one px call by mapping DataFrame columns to x, y and other arguments.
concepts.why: Plotly Express is the fastest way to an interactive chart and covers most everyday plotting.
concepts.body:
Plotly Express functions take a DataFrame and column names:

```python
px.scatter(df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp")
px.line(df, x="date", y="price")
px.bar(df, x="country", y="pop")
```

Each returns a complete `Figure` with axis titles taken from the column names, hover tooltips showing the mapped values, and a default theme. Display it with `fig.show()` in a notebook or script, or save it with `fig.write_html(...)`.

Express accepts pandas DataFrames and, through the narwhals compatibility layer, also Polars and PyArrow tables. You can also pass plain lists or arrays: `px.line(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[2, 4, 3])`.

Common arguments shared by most functions:

- `title=`, `labels={"gdpPercap": "GDP per capita"}` to rename columns in axis titles, legends and tooltips;
- `log_x=True` / `log_y=True`, `range_x=[0, 10]`;
- `width=`, `height=` in pixels;
- `template="plotly_white"` for a lighter look.

`px.line` connects points in the order of the rows, so sort by x first. With `y=["a", "b"]` (several columns) Express draws one trace per column from wide-form data.

`px.data` ships sample datasets (`gapminder`, `tips`, `iris`, `stocks`) bundled with the library, handy for experimenting offline.
concepts.code:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("year == 2007")
print(df.shape)                              # (142, 8)

fig = px.scatter(df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", log_x=True,
                 labels={"gdpPercap": "GDP per capita",
                         "lifeExp": "Life expectancy"},
                 title="Wealth and health, 2007")
print(fig.layout.xaxis.title.text)           # GDP per capita
print(fig.layout.xaxis.type)                 # log
print(len(fig.data), fig.data[0].mode)       # 1 markers

stocks = px.data.stocks()
fig2 = px.line(stocks, x="date", y=["GOOG", "AAPL"])   # wide form
print([t.name for t in fig2.data])           # ['GOOG', 'AAPL']
fig.write_html("gapminder.html")
takeaways: px functions take a DataFrame plus column names and return a Figure
`labels=` renames columns everywhere they appear
Passing several y columns draws one trace per column
pitfalls: Plotting unsorted data with `px.line`, which connects rows in their given order.

options: An error: y must be one column
One trace with two y values per point
quiz.explain: Express treats a list of y columns as wide-form data and creates one trace for each.

concepts.name: Distributions and part-of-whole charts
concepts.summary: Use px.histogram, box, violin, strip and ecdf for distributions, and pie, sunburst and treemap for parts of a whole.
concepts.why: Choosing the right chart type for the question is half of good visualization, and Express offers dozens with a consistent API.
concepts.body:
Plotly Express uses the same arguments across many chart types, so learning one teaches them all.

For **distributions**:

- `px.histogram(df, x="total_bill", nbins=30)` bins and counts. It can also aggregate: `px.histogram(df, x="day", y="tip", histfunc="sum")` sums tips per day, which is often the quickest way to make a bar chart of totals. `histnorm="percent"` normalizes.
- `px.box`, `px.violin` and `px.strip` compare distributions across categories; `points="all"` overlays raw observations on a box or violin.
- `px.ecdf` shows cumulative proportions without binning choices.
- `marginal="box"` (or `"violin"`, `"rug"`, `"histogram"`) on `scatter` or `histogram` adds a small distribution plot on the edge.

For **parts of a whole**:

- `px.pie(df, names="category", values="amount")`; use `hole=0.4` for a donut. Pies only work with a handful of slices.
- `px.sunburst` and `px.treemap` show hierarchies: `path=["region", "country"]` nests the levels, and clicking a segment zooms in.

Other families include `px.density_heatmap` and `px.density_contour` for many points, `px.imshow` for matrices and images, `px.scatter_3d`, polar, ternary and geographic charts, and `px.timeline` for Gantt charts.

Prefer bars to pies when comparing similar values: people judge lengths more accurately than angles.
concepts.code:
import plotly.express as px

tips = px.data.tips()
print(tips.shape)                                    # (244, 7)

fig = px.histogram(tips, x="total_bill", nbins=20, marginal="box")
print(len(fig.data), fig.data[1].type)               # 2 box

totals = px.histogram(tips, x="day", y="tip", histfunc="sum")
print(totals.data[0].histfunc)                       # sum

box = px.box(tips, x="day", y="total_bill", points="all")
print(box.data[0].boxpoints)                         # all

tree = px.treemap(tips, path=["day", "time"], values="total_bill")
print(tree.data[0].type)                             # treemap
fig.write_html("bills.html")
takeaways: histogram, box, violin, strip and ecdf cover distributions
`histogram` with `y` and `histfunc` aggregates, like a quick group-by bar chart
sunburst and treemap show hierarchies via `path=`
pitfalls: Using a pie with many similar slices, which is much harder to read than a sorted bar chart.

quiz.q: Which call gives a bar per day with the total tip amount?
quiz.explain: histogram groups by x and applies histfunc to y, here summing tips per day.

concepts.name: Color, symbols, facets and hover data
concepts.summary: Map more columns to color, symbol and size, split charts into facet panels, and choose what the hover tooltip shows.
concepts.why: Encoding extra variables and faceting is how you compare groups in one figure instead of many.
concepts.code:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("year in [1987, 2007]")
fig = px.scatter(
    df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", log_x=True,
    color="continent", size="pop", size_max=40,
    facet_col="year", hover_name="country",
    hover_data={"pop": ":,", "continent": False},
    category_orders={"continent": ["Europe", "Asia", "Americas", "Africa", "Oceania"]},
)
fig.for_each_annotation(lambda a: a.update(text=a.text.split("=")[1]))

print(list(dict.fromkeys(t.name for t in fig.data)))
# ['Europe', 'Asia', 'Americas', 'Africa', 'Oceania']
print(len(fig.data))                     # 10: 5 continents x 2 facets
print([a.text for a in fig.layout.annotations])   # ['1987', '2007']
fig.write_html("facets.html")
takeaways: Categorical `color` creates one trace per group; numeric `color` creates a color scale
`facet_col`/`facet_row` split into panels; `category_orders` fixes ordering
`hover_name` and `hover_data` decide the tooltip contents
pitfalls: Mapping an ID-like column with hundreds of values to `color`, creating hundreds of traces and a huge legend.

quiz.q: You set `color='continent'` on a scatter of 5 continents. How many traces does the figure contain (no facets)?
quiz.explain: Express creates one trace per value of a categorical color column.

concepts.name: Updating layout, axes and legends
concepts.summary: Change titles, axis ranges and formats, legends, margins and size with update_layout, update_xaxes and update_yaxes.
concepts.why: Almost every chart needs tweaks after creation, and these update methods are the standard way to make them.
concepts.body:
Plotly figures are edited after creation through `update_*` methods that take keyword arguments and return the figure, so they chain:

```python
fig.update_layout(title_text="Revenue", height=400, legend_title_text="Region")
fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Month", tickangle=-45)
fig.update_yaxes(tickprefix="$", tickformat=",.0f", rangemode="tozero")
```

**Magic underscores** let you reach nested attributes in one keyword: `title_font_size=20` is the same as `title=dict(font=dict(size=20))`. Updates are merged, not replaced, so changing `title_font_size` keeps the title text.

`update_xaxes` and `update_yaxes` apply to all axes at once, which matters for faceted figures with many axes; pass `row=`, `col=` or `selector=` to target some of them.

Frequently used settings:

- axes: `range=[lo, hi]`, `type="log"`, `tickformat` (d3-format, e.g. `".1%"`, `",.0f"`), `dtick`, `showgrid`, `zeroline`, `matches=None` to unlink facet axes;
- legend: `orientation="h"`, `x`, `y`, `xanchor`, `yanchor`, `showlegend=False`;
- `margin=dict(l=40, r=20, t=50, b=40)`, `width`, `height`;
- `hovermode="x unified"` for one tooltip listing all traces at an x.

Assigning attributes directly also works: `fig.layout.title.text = "Revenue"`.
concepts.code:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.stocks()
fig = px.line(df, x="date", y=["GOOG", "MSFT"])

(fig.update_layout(title_text="Stocks normalized to 1 at start",
                   title_font_size=20, legend_title_text="Ticker",
                   legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.02, x=0, yanchor="bottom"),
                   hovermode="x unified", height=420)
    .update_xaxes(title_text=None, dtick="M3", tickformat="%b %Y")
    .update_yaxes(tickformat=".0%", title_text="Relative price"))

print(fig.layout.title.text)          # Stocks normalized to 1 at start
print(fig.layout.title.font.size)     # 20
print(fig.layout.yaxis.tickformat)    # .0%
fig.write_html("stocks.html")
takeaways: `update_layout`, `update_xaxes`, `update_yaxes` merge changes and chain
Magic underscores reach nested attributes: `title_font_size=20`
Tick formats use d3-format strings such as `,.0f` and `.1%`
pitfalls: Calling `fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=...)` on a faceted figure and only changing the first panel; use `update_xaxes`.

quiz.explain: Underscores in keyword names step into nested attributes: title -> font -> color.

concepts.name: Showing and exporting figures
concepts.summary: Display figures with renderers, save interactive HTML, and export static PNG, SVG or PDF images with Kaleido.
concepts.why: A chart is only useful once it reaches its audience, whether in a notebook, a shared HTML file or a slide.
concepts.body:
`fig.show()` displays a figure using a **renderer** chosen for your environment: inline in Jupyter, VS Code and Colab, or a new browser tab when run as a script. `plotly.io.renderers.default` reports or sets it (`"browser"`, `"notebook"`, `"vscode"`, `"png"` ...).

**Interactive HTML** keeps all interactivity and needs no server:

```python
fig.write_html("chart.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn")
```

`include_plotlyjs=True` (the default) embeds the whole plotly.js library, about 4-5 MB, so the file works offline; `"cdn"` loads it from the internet, making files tiny. `full_html=False` produces a `<div>` snippet to embed in an existing page. `fig.to_html()` returns the string instead of writing a file.

**Static images** come from **Kaleido**, a separate package (`pip install kaleido`), version 1 or later in Plotly 7. Kaleido 1 drives a headless Chrome, so a Chrome or Chromium installation is needed; `plotly_get_chrome` (installed with Plotly) downloads a compatible one.

```python
fig.write_image("chart.png", scale=2)   # also .svg, .pdf, .jpg, .webp
```

`width`, `height` and `scale` control the output size; `scale=2` doubles resolution for crisp slides.

The **config** argument controls the in-browser toolbar: `fig.show(config={"displayModeBar": False})` hides it, and `{"toImageButtonOptions": {"format": "svg"}}` changes what the camera button downloads.
concepts.code:
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.io as pio
import os

fig = px.bar(x=["a", "b", "c"], y=[4, 2, 5], title="Exports")

fig.write_html("embedded.html")                         # self-contained
fig.write_html("cdn.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn")      # needs internet
print(os.path.getsize("embedded.html") > 1_000_000)     # True: includes plotly.js
print(os.path.getsize("cdn.html") < 20_000)             # True

snippet = fig.to_html(full_html=False, include_plotlyjs=False)
print(snippet.lstrip().startswith("<div"))              # True: embeddable fragment

print(list(pio.renderers)[:3])          # e.g. ['plotly_mimetype', 'jupyterlab', 'nteract']
# fig.write_image("chart.png", scale=2) # needs kaleido>=1 and Chrome
# fig.show(config={"displayModeBar": False})
takeaways: `fig.show()` uses an environment-specific renderer
`write_html` keeps interactivity; `include_plotlyjs='cdn'` keeps files small
`write_image` needs Kaleido 1+ and a Chrome install for PNG, SVG and PDF
pitfalls: Emailing an HTML file written with include_plotlyjs='cdn' to someone offline, who then sees a blank page.

quiz.q: You need a single HTML file that works on an air-gapped laptop. Which option is right?
quiz.explain: Only embedding plotly.js makes the file self-contained; the other options load it from elsewhere or omit it.

concepts.name: Graph objects: building figures trace by trace
concepts.summary: Construct figures with go.Figure and add_trace for full control over trace types and properties.
concepts.why: Graph objects handle what Express cannot: mixing trace types, custom per-trace styling and charts assembled in loops.
concepts.body:
`plotly.graph_objects` (imported as `go`) has a class for every trace type: `go.Scatter` (used for lines and markers alike), `go.Bar`, `go.Histogram`, `go.Box`, `go.Heatmap`, `go.Pie`, `go.Scattergl`, `go.Candlestick` and many more. Build a figure by adding traces:

```python
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines+markers", name="actual"))
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=x, y=forecast, name="forecast", opacity=0.5))
```

Key points:

- `go.Scatter` draws lines, markers or both through `mode`: `"lines"`, `"markers"`, `"lines+markers"`, `"text"`.
- Each trace has its own `name` (legend entry), `marker`, `line`, `hovertemplate`, `showlegend` and `legendgroup`.
- Traces are drawn in the order added, so later traces sit on top.
- Arguments can be nested dicts (`marker=dict(color="red", size=8)`) or classes (`go.scatter.Marker(...)`).

Mix with Express freely: start from `px.scatter(...)` and call `fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(...))` to add a reference curve, or take Express traces from one figure (`fig_a.data`) and add them to another.

Use Express when your data is a tidy DataFrame and the chart maps columns to roles. Switch to graph objects when combining different trace types, building traces in a loop from non-tabular data, or when you need a trace type Express does not wrap.
concepts.code:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px

months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May"]
actual = [120, 135, 128, 150, 162]
target = [125, 130, 135, 140, 145]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=months, y=actual, name="actual", marker_color="#3F4F75"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=months, y=target, name="target",
                         mode="lines+markers", line=dict(dash="dash", color="orange")))
print([t.type for t in fig.data])         # ['bar', 'scatter']

base = px.scatter(x=[1, 2, 3, 4], y=[1, 4, 9, 16])
base.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 4], y=[1, 16], mode="lines", name="chord"))
print(len(base.data), base.data[1].mode)  # 2 lines
fig.write_html("target.html")
takeaways: Every trace type has a go class; add them with `fig.add_trace`
`go.Scatter` covers lines and markers via `mode`
Mix freely: refine Express figures with added graph-object traces
pitfalls: Looking for go.Line; lines are go.Scatter with mode='lines'.

quiz.q: How do you draw a line chart with graph objects?
quiz.explain: There is no Line trace; Scatter with mode='lines' draws connected lines.

concepts.name: Styling traces and hover templates
concepts.summary: Change trace properties in bulk with update_traces and selectors, and write custom tooltips with hovertemplate.
concepts.why: Consistent styling and clear tooltips are what make interactive charts feel professional rather than default.
concepts.body:
`fig.update_traces(...)` sets properties on every trace, or only those matched by a selector: ```python fig.update_traces(marker_size=8, selector=dict(type="scatter")) fig.update_traces(line_width=3, selector=dict(name="forecast")) ``` `fig.for_each_trace(fn)` calls a function per trace, useful for logic like renaming: `fig.for_each_trace(lambda t: t.update(name=t.name.title()))`. Direct access also works: `fig.data[0].marker.color = "red"`. **Hover templates** define the tooltip exactly. Inside `hovertemplate`, `%{x}`, `%{y}`, `%{text}` and `%{customdata[0]}` insert values, with optional d3 formats after a colon: `%{y:$,.2f}`, `%{x|%b %d, %Y}` for dates. `
` breaks lines and `` makes text bold. The secondary box with the trace name is controlled by ``: leaving it empty hides that box. `customdata` attaches extra per-point values to a trace, usually a 2D array of columns, so tooltips can show fields that are not plotted. Express does this automatically for `hover_data` columns. Related layout options: `hovermode` (`"closest"`, `"x"`, `"x unified"`), `hoverlabel=dict(bgcolor="white", font_size=12)`, and `hoverinfo="skip"` on a trace that should never show a tooltip. Express already writes a hovertemplate; `update_traces(hovertemplate=...)` replaces it completely, so include every value you want shown.
concepts.code:
import plotly.express as px df = px.data.gapminder().query("year == 2007 and continent == 'Europe'") fig = px.scatter(df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", text="iso_alpha", custom_data=["country", "pop"]) fig.update_traces( marker=dict(size=10, color="#3F4F75", line=dict(width=1, color="white")), textposition="top center", hovertemplate=("%{customdata[0]}
" "GDP: %{x:$,.0f}
Life exp.: %{y:.1f} yrs
" "Pop: %{customdata[1]:,}"), selector=dict(type="scatter"), ) t = fig.data[0] print(t.marker.size, t.customdata.shape) # 10 (30, 2) print(t.hovertemplate.endswith("")) # True fig.write_html("europe.html")
takeaways: `update_traces` with `selector=` styles some or all traces at once
`hovertemplate` uses `%{field:format}` and `<extra></extra>` hides the trace box
`customdata` carries extra per-point values into tooltips
pitfalls: Replacing an Express hovertemplate and forgetting the fields it used to show.

quiz.q: In a hovertemplate, what does `<extra></extra>` do?
options: Adds an extra line with all columns
Hides the secondary box that normally shows the trace name
quiz.explain: The <extra> tag holds the secondary hover label content; leaving it empty removes that box.

concepts.name: Subplots and secondary y axes
concepts.summary: Combine different charts in one figure with make_subplots, including mixed trace types and secondary y axes.
concepts.why: Dashboards and reports often need different chart types side by side, which Express facets cannot produce.
concepts.body:
`plotly.subplots.make_subplots(rows, cols)` creates a figure with a grid of axes. Add traces to a cell with `row=` and `col=`:

```python
fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("Revenue", "Users"))
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=m, y=rev), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=m, y=users), row=1, col=2)
```

Options:

- `shared_xaxes=True` / `shared_yaxes=True` link axes; `vertical_spacing` and `horizontal_spacing` set gaps as fractions;
- `column_widths=[0.7, 0.3]` and `row_heights=[...]` for unequal sizes;
- `specs` describes each cell: `{"colspan": 2}` to span, `None` for empty, `{"type": "domain"}` for pie-like traces that have no x/y axes, `{"secondary_y": True}` for a second y axis.

A **secondary y axis** puts two scales on one panel:

```python
fig = make_subplots(specs=[[{"secondary_y": True}]])
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(...), secondary_y=False)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(...), secondary_y=True)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Rate", secondary_y=True)
```

In Plotly 7, overlaying y axes default to `tickmode="sync"`, so both axes share gridline positions; set `tickmode="auto"` on the secondary axis for independent ticks.

Axis updates target cells with `fig.update_xaxes(..., row=2, col=1)`. Internally the axes are named `xaxis`, `xaxis2`, `yaxis3` ..., which you see in `fig.layout`.
concepts.code:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

m = ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"]
fig = make_subplots(
    rows=1, cols=2, column_widths=[0.65, 0.35],
    specs=[[{"secondary_y": True}, {"type": "domain"}]],
    subplot_titles=("Revenue and margin", "Revenue by channel"),
)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=m, y=[10, 14, 13, 18], name="revenue"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=m, y=[0.21, 0.24, 0.22, 0.27], name="margin"),
              row=1, col=1, secondary_y=True)
fig.add_trace(go.Pie(labels=["web", "store"], values=[35, 20]), row=1, col=2)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Revenue ($M)", secondary_y=False)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Margin", tickformat=".0%", secondary_y=True)

print(fig.data[1].yaxis)               # y2
print(fig.layout.yaxis2.overlaying)    # y
print([round(v, 2) for v in fig.data[2].domain.x])  # [0.68, 0.94]: right column
fig.write_html("quarterly.html")
takeaways: `make_subplots` + `add_trace(..., row=, col=)` builds mixed-chart grids
`specs` sets cell types, spans and secondary y axes
Pie-like traces need `{'type': 'domain'}` cells
pitfalls: Adding a pie trace to a regular xy cell, which raises an error about the subplot type.

quiz.q: You want bars for revenue and a line for growth rate on different y scales in one panel. What do you use?
options: make_subplots(specs=[[{'secondary_y': True}]]) and secondary_y=True for the line
quiz.explain: A secondary y axis overlays a second independent scale on the same panel.

concepts.name: Reference lines, shapes and annotations
concepts.summary: Highlight thresholds, periods and points with add_hline, add_vrect, add_shape and add_annotation.
concepts.why: Annotations direct attention to what matters, such as a target, an incident window or an outlier.
concepts.body:
Plotly has convenience methods for the most common highlights:

- `fig.add_hline(y=100, line_dash="dash", annotation_text="target")` and `fig.add_vline(x=...)` draw lines across the whole plot.
- `fig.add_hrect(y0=..., y1=...)` and `fig.add_vrect(x0="2026-03-01", x1="2026-03-08", fillcolor="red", opacity=0.15, line_width=0)` shade bands, ideal for incidents or weekends.
- `fig.add_annotation(x=..., y=..., text="peak", showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, ax=0, ay=-40)` labels a point; `ax`/`ay` are the arrow tail offset in pixels.

On faceted or subplot figures these accept `row=` and `col=` (or `"all"`) to target panels.

Under the hood they add entries to `fig.layout.shapes` and `fig.layout.annotations`. Positions are interpreted through `xref` and `yref`: `"x"`/`"y"` mean data coordinates, `"paper"` means fractions of the plotting area (0 to 1), and `"x domain"` means fractions of one axis's domain. `add_hline` uses `xref="x domain"` so the line always spans the full width regardless of zoom.

`add_shape(type="rect" | "line" | "circle" | "path", ...)` draws arbitrary shapes, and `layer="below"` puts them behind the data. `fig.add_layout_image` places logos.

Annotations also work as free text, for example a source note at `xref="paper", yref="paper", x=0, y=-0.15`.
concepts.code:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.stocks()
fig = px.line(df, x="date", y="AAPL")

fig.add_hline(y=1.0, line_dash="dash", line_color="gray",
              annotation_text="start value", annotation_position="bottom right")
fig.add_vrect(x0="2018-10-01", x1="2018-12-31", fillcolor="red",
              opacity=0.12, line_width=0, annotation_text="Q4 selloff")
peak = df.loc[df["AAPL"].idxmax()]
fig.add_annotation(x=peak["date"], y=peak["AAPL"], text="peak",
                   showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, ax=0, ay=-40)
fig.add_annotation(text="Source: px.data.stocks", xref="paper", yref="paper",
                   x=0, y=-0.15, showarrow=False)

print(len(fig.layout.shapes), len(fig.layout.annotations))  # 2 4
print(fig.layout.shapes[0].xref)                           # x domain
fig.write_html("annotated.html")
takeaways: `add_hline`/`add_vline`/`add_hrect`/`add_vrect` cover most highlights
`add_annotation` labels points; `ax`/`ay` offset the arrow in pixels
`xref`/`yref` choose data, paper or axis-domain coordinates
pitfalls: Positioning a note with data coordinates when it should stay fixed relative to the plot area (use xref='paper').

quiz.q: You want a caption below the plot area that does not move when the user zooms. Which reference do you use?
quiz.explain: Paper coordinates are relative to the plotting area and ignore data ranges and zoom.

concepts.name: Animated charts with frames
concepts.summary: Animate figures over time with animation_frame in Express, and understand frames, sliders and play buttons.
concepts.why: Animations show change over time memorably, as in the classic Gapminder chart, with a single extra argument.
concepts.body:
In Plotly Express, adding `animation_frame="year"` creates one **frame** per value of that column, plus a slider and play/pause buttons. `animation_group="country"` tells Plotly which points are the same object across frames, so they move smoothly instead of reappearing.

```python
px.scatter(df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", size="pop", color="continent",
           animation_frame="year", animation_group="country",
           range_x=[100, 100_000], range_y=[25, 90], log_x=True)
```

Always set `range_x` and `range_y`: axis ranges are computed for the first frame only, so later data can fly off the chart.

Under the hood the figure gets `fig.frames`, a list of `go.Frame` objects each holding its own `data` (and optionally `layout`), plus `layout.updatemenus` (the buttons) and `layout.sliders`. The initial `fig.data` is the first frame. You can build this yourself with graph objects for custom animations, and change speed through the button's animation arguments:

```python
fig.layout.updatemenus[0].buttons[0].args[1]["frame"]["duration"] = 300
```

Plotly animates by interpolating between frames, which works well for scatter and bar traces; other trace types may just jump between states.

Animations suit exploration and presentations; for printed reports, small multiples (facets) of a few chosen years usually communicate better.
concepts.code:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder()
fig = px.scatter(
    df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", size="pop", size_max=45,
    color="continent", hover_name="country", log_x=True,
    animation_frame="year", animation_group="country",
    range_x=[200, 60_000], range_y=[25, 90],
)
print(len(fig.frames))                       # 12: one per year
print(fig.frames[0].name, fig.frames[-1].name)   # 1952 2007
print(len(fig.layout.sliders[0].steps))      # 12
print(fig.layout.updatemenus[0].buttons[0].method) # animate (the play button)

fig.layout.updatemenus[0].buttons[0].args[1]["frame"]["duration"] = 300
fig.write_html("gapminder_anim.html")
takeaways: `animation_frame` creates frames, a slider and play buttons
`animation_group` keeps object identity across frames
Fix `range_x`/`range_y`, since ranges come from the first frame
pitfalls: Leaving axis ranges automatic, so points leave the visible area in later frames.

quiz.q: Why should you set `range_y` on an animated px chart?
options: Animations require it or they raise an error
Axis ranges are fitted to the first frame only
quiz.explain: Ranges are not recomputed per frame, so later values can fall outside the initial range.

concepts.name: Maps: choropleths and point maps
concepts.summary: Plot geographic data with choropleth and scatter_geo, and tile-based maps with scatter_map and choropleth_map.
concepts.why: Location is a natural dimension for business and public data, and Plotly makes interactive maps a one-liner.
concepts.body:
Plotly has two families of maps.

**Outline (geo) maps** draw country and region shapes without a tile server: `px.choropleth` colors regions, and `px.scatter_geo` / `px.line_geo` place points and lines.

```python
px.choropleth(df, locations="iso_alpha", color="lifeExp",
              hover_name="country", projection="natural earth")
```

`locations` are matched by `locationmode`: ISO-3 codes by default, or `"USA-states"` for two-letter state codes. Country names are supported but matched strictly in Plotly 7, so prefer ISO-3 codes. For other regions, pass a GeoJSON `geojson=` and `featureidkey="properties.id"` to say which property matches your `locations` column. Since Plotly 7, geo maps zoom to fit the plotted locations by default (`fitbounds="locations"`).

**Tile maps** draw on a street-map background rendered by MapLibre: `px.scatter_map(df, lat="lat", lon="lon", zoom=10)`, `px.density_map` for heatmaps of many points, `px.choropleth_map` for GeoJSON regions on tiles. Choose the background with `map_style` (`"open-street-map"`, `"carto-positron"`, `"carto-darkmatter"` ...); these need no access token. The older Mapbox-based functions (`scatter_mapbox` and friends) were removed in Plotly 7.

Use a sequential color scale for quantities and normalize by population or area: raw counts on a choropleth mostly show where people live.
concepts.code:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("year == 2007")
fig = px.choropleth(df, locations="iso_alpha", color="lifeExp",
                    hover_name="country", color_continuous_scale="Viridis",
                    projection="natural earth")
print(fig.data[0].type, fig.data[0].locationmode)    # choropleth None (plotly.js default: ISO-3)

cities = px.data.carshare()                          # Montreal car-share points
tiles = px.scatter_map(cities, lat="centroid_lat", lon="centroid_lon",
                       color="peak_hour", size="car_hours", size_max=12,
                       zoom=10, map_style="carto-positron")
print(tiles.data[0].type)                            # scattermap
print(tiles.layout.map.style)                        # carto-positron
fig.write_html("life_map.html")
tiles.write_html("carshare.html")
takeaways: Geo maps (choropleth, scatter_geo) need no tiles; tile maps use MapLibre
Match regions by ISO-3 codes, state codes, or GeoJSON with `featureidkey`
In Plotly 7 use `scatter_map`/`choropleth_map`; the mapbox functions are gone
pitfalls: Mapping raw counts on a choropleth, which mostly reflects population rather than the rate you care about.

quiz.q: Your regions are custom sales territories defined in a GeoJSON file. What do you pass to px.choropleth?
options: geojson=... and featureidkey pointing at the id property
lat and lon of each territory's center
quiz.explain: Custom shapes come from your GeoJSON, matched to the locations column via featureidkey.

concepts.name: Templates and theming
concepts.summary: Apply built-in templates, create a custom house template, and set it as the default for all figures.
concepts.why: A shared template gives every chart in a product or report the same fonts, colors and layout without repeating settings.
concepts.body:
A **template** is a figure-shaped bundle of defaults: a `layout` (fonts, colorway, background, axis styles) and per-trace-type `data` defaults. Built-ins live in `plotly.io.templates`: `"plotly"` (the default), `"plotly_white"`, `"plotly_dark"`, `"simple_white"`, `"ggplot2"`, `"seaborn"`, `"presentation"` and `"none"`.

Use one per figure with `template="plotly_white"`, or globally:

```python
import plotly.io as pio
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
```

Make your own by creating a `go.layout.Template` and registering it:

```python
pio.templates["house"] = go.layout.Template(
    layout=dict(font_family="Inter", colorway=["#3F4F75", "#E8A33D"],
                title_x=0.02))
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white+house"
```

The `+` syntax **composes** templates left to right, so you only define the differences from a base.

Values set explicitly on a figure always win over the template. Templates only fill in what is not set, which is why `colorway` changes the default trace colors but not traces you colored yourself. Express functions also read `px.defaults` (`px.defaults.template`, `px.defaults.width`, `px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence`), handy for notebook-wide settings.

Template trace defaults are matched by trace type and cycle when there are several, which allows, for example, alternating marker symbols. A template can also include annotations such as a watermark or a logo image that appear on every figure.
concepts.code:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.io as pio
import plotly.express as px

pio.templates["house"] = go.layout.Template(
    layout=dict(font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", size=13),
                colorway=["#3F4F75", "#E8A33D", "#4BA3A3"],
                title=dict(x=0.02),
                annotations=[dict(text="ACME analytics", showarrow=False,
                                  xref="paper", yref="paper", x=1, y=-0.18,
                                  font=dict(size=10, color="gray"))]))
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white+house"

fig = px.bar(x=["a", "b"], y=[3, 5], color=["a", "b"])
print(fig.data[0].marker.color)                 # #3F4F75 (from colorway)
print(fig.layout.template.layout.font.family)   # Inter, sans-serif
print(fig.layout.template.layout.plot_bgcolor)  # white (from plotly_white)

red = px.bar(x=["a"], y=[1], color_discrete_sequence=["red"])
print(red.data[0].marker.color)                 # red: explicit beats template
takeaways: Templates bundle layout and trace defaults; built-ins are in `pio.templates`
Register a custom `go.layout.Template` and compose with `base+house`
Explicit figure settings always override template values
pitfalls: Expecting a new template to recolor traces whose colors were set explicitly.

options: Merges both templates, with house overriding plotly_white where they overlap
Raises an error: only one template is allowed
Uses house only for traces and plotly_white for layout
quiz.explain: The + syntax composes templates left to right; later ones override earlier ones.

concepts.name: Buttons, sliders, range selectors and events
concepts.summary: Add in-chart interactivity with updatemenus, sliders, range sliders and selectors, and react to clicks with FigureWidget.
concepts.why: Self-contained HTML charts can still let readers switch views, filter and zoom without any server.
concepts.code:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.stocks()
fig = go.Figure([go.Scatter(x=df.date, y=df[t], name=t) for t in ["GOOG", "AAPL", "AMZN"]])

buttons = [dict(label="All", method="update",
                args=[{"visible": [True, True, True]}, {"title.text": "All"}])]
for i, t in enumerate(["GOOG", "AAPL", "AMZN"]):
    vis = [j == i for j in range(3)]
    buttons.append(dict(label=t, method="update", args=[{"visible": vis}, {"title.text": t}]))

fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, x=0, y=1.15)])
fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True, rangeselector=dict(buttons=[
    dict(count=6, label="6m", step="month", stepmode="backward"),
    dict(count=1, label="1y", step="year", stepmode="backward"),
    dict(step="all")]))

print([b.label for b in fig.layout.updatemenus[0].buttons])  # ['All', 'GOOG', 'AAPL', 'AMZN']
print(fig.layout.xaxis.rangeslider.visible)                   # True
fig.write_html("controls.html")    # works offline, no Python needed
takeaways: updatemenus and sliders call restyle, relayout, update or animate in the browser
Range sliders and selectors make time series navigable
Python callbacks need FigureWidget, Dash or Streamlit, not a static file
pitfalls: Expecting a button in an exported HTML file to run Python code; it can only change the existing figure.

quiz.q: A dropdown should show one of three traces at a time. Which method and args fit?
quiz.explain: Trace visibility is a trace property, changed with restyle or update.

concepts.name: Plotly in apps: Dash, Streamlit and widgets
concepts.summary: Embed Plotly figures in web apps and notebooks with Dash, Streamlit, FigureWidget or plain HTML and JSON.
concepts.why: Most production Plotly charts live inside an app or a web page, not in a notebook.
concepts.body:
Because a figure is JSON for plotly.js, you can deliver it anywhere JavaScript runs.

**Dash** (from Plotly) builds web apps in pure Python. A figure goes into `dcc.Graph(figure=fig)`, and callbacks regenerate figures when inputs change or when users click, select or zoom (`Input("graph", "clickData")`).

**Streamlit** renders a figure with `st.plotly_chart(fig)`; widgets above it rerun the script with new inputs. Selections can be returned with `on_select="rerun"`.

**Jupyter**: figures display inline by default. `go.FigureWidget(fig)` makes a live widget that Python can update in place and listen to.

**Any web stack**: send `fig.to_json()` from an API and call `Plotly.newPlot(div, fig.data, fig.layout)` in the browser, or embed `fig.to_html(full_html=False, include_plotlyjs="cdn")` in a server-rendered template. `plotly.io.from_json` and `pio.read_json` load a figure back.

Practical concerns:

- Size: large arrays bloat JSON; aggregate on the server before sending.
- Versions: the plotly.js version in the page must match what the Python library generated; mixing a very old CDN version with a new figure causes missing features.
- Responsiveness: set `config={"responsive": True}` and avoid fixed `width` so charts resize with their container.
- Updates: in apps, regenerate or patch figures rather than creating new ones per tiny change (Dash has `Patch` for partial updates).
concepts.code:
import json
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.io as pio

fig = px.line(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[3, 1, 2], title="API chart")

payload = fig.to_json()                  # send from your web API
spec = json.loads(payload)
print(sorted(spec))                      # ['data', 'layout']

restored = pio.from_json(payload)        # e.g. in a test or another service
print(restored.layout.title.text)        # API chart

snippet = fig.to_html(full_html=False, include_plotlyjs="cdn",
                      config={"responsive": True, "displaylogo": False})
print("cdn.plot.ly" in snippet)          # True: loads plotly.js from the CDN

# Browser side:  Plotly.newPlot("chart", spec.data, spec.layout)
# Dash:          dcc.Graph(figure=fig)
# Streamlit:     st.plotly_chart(fig, on_select="rerun")
takeaways: A figure is JSON: send it to any page that loads plotly.js
Dash (`dcc.Graph`) and Streamlit (`st.plotly_chart`) embed figures in Python apps
Keep payloads small and plotly.js versions consistent
pitfalls: Shipping a figure with a million raw points through a web API instead of aggregating first.

quiz.q: Your FastAPI backend should give a React front end a chart. What is the simplest contract?
options: Return fig.to_json() and render it with Plotly.newPlot on the client
Return the Python pickle of the Figure
quiz.explain: The JSON spec is exactly what plotly.js needs on the client; it stays interactive.

concepts.name: Performance: WebGL, data size and serialization
concepts.summary: Render hundreds of thousands of points with WebGL traces, shrink figure payloads, and know when to aggregate instead.
concepts.why: Interactive charts run in the browser, so data volume directly drives load time, memory and responsiveness.
concepts.body:
Default SVG traces create a DOM element per point and slow down beyond tens of thousands of points. Options, roughly in order:

- **WebGL traces**: `go.Scattergl` instead of `go.Scatter`, or `render_mode="webgl"` in `px.scatter`/`px.line`. Express already switches to WebGL automatically above about 1000 points. WebGL handles around a million points, but browsers limit the number of WebGL contexts per page (often 8-16), so pages with many WebGL charts can fail.
- **Heatmap-style traces**: `px.density_heatmap`, `go.Histogram2d` or `px.imshow` of a pre-binned grid send a fixed-size grid instead of every point.
- **Aggregate or sample server-side** (pandas `resample`, datashader for rasterizing millions of points into an image).

**Payload size**: Plotly 6+ serializes NumPy arrays as base64 typed arrays (`{"dtype": "f8", "bdata": ...}`) rather than decimal text, which is smaller and faster to parse. Use compact dtypes (`float32`, small ints) to shrink them further, and avoid object or string columns where numbers suffice. Unused `customdata` and long hover texts add up too.

**Python-side cost**: graph-object validation is thorough but slow for thousands of traces. Build fewer, larger traces; for very large generated figures you can keep the spec as plain dicts and serialize with `plotly.io.to_json(spec, validate=False)`, at the cost of losing error checking. `fig.to_dict()` copies data, so avoid calling it repeatedly in loops.

Measure with `len(fig.to_json())` and the browser's performance tools.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.graph_objects as go

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=200_000)
y = rng.normal(size=200_000)

fig = px.scatter(x=x, y=y)
print(fig.data[0].type)                          # scattergl (auto for large data)

j64 = go.Figure(go.Scattergl(x=x, y=y, mode="markers")).to_json()
j32 = go.Figure(go.Scattergl(x=x.astype("float32"), y=y.astype("float32"),
                             mode="markers")).to_json()
print('"bdata"' in j64)                           # True: base64 typed arrays
print(round(len(j32) / len(j64), 2))              # about 0.5: float32 halves payload

heat = px.density_heatmap(x=x, y=y, nbinsx=100, nbinsy=100)
print(len(heat.to_json()) < len(j32) / 10)        # False: raw points still sent

agg, xe, ye = np.histogram2d(x, y, bins=100)
img = px.imshow(agg.T, origin="lower")            # send only a 100x100 grid
print(len(img.to_json()) < len(j32) / 10)         # True
takeaways: Use WebGL traces (`Scattergl`, `render_mode='webgl'`) for large point clouds
Aggregate server-side: a 100x100 grid beats a million points
NumPy arrays serialize as base64 typed arrays; smaller dtypes mean smaller payloads
pitfalls: Putting dozens of WebGL charts on one page and hitting the browser's WebGL context limit.

quiz.q: Why is `px.density_heatmap(x=x, y=y)` not a payload fix for 5 million points?
options: It does not support large data
The browser still receives every raw point and bins them in plotly.js
quiz.explain: histogram2d-style traces bin on the client, so the raw arrays are still serialized; pre-bin in Python to send only the grid.

concepts.name: Figure JSON, validation and plotly.js internals
concepts.summary: Understand how Python figures map to the plotly.js schema, how defaults are filled in, and how to inspect the fully resolved figure.
concepts.why: Debugging odd rendering, writing generic chart code or interoperating with JavaScript requires knowing what plotly.js actually receives.
concepts.body:
The Python graph-object classes are **generated from the plotly.js schema**, a JSON description of every trace type and attribute with its type, allowed values and default. That is why validation errors list every valid property and why each Python release pins a specific plotly.js version (`plotly.offline.get_plotlyjs_version()`).

What you build in Python is only the **explicit** part of the figure. When plotly.js draws it, it fills in defaults from the schema, the template and computed values (autoranges, tick positions, axis types guessed from the data). So `fig.layout.xaxis.range` is `None` in Python even though the chart has a range. `fig.full_figure_for_development()` runs plotly.js through Kaleido and returns the fully resolved figure, the way to see what was actually used.

Other internals worth knowing:

- Each Python attribute set is validated and **coerced** (lists to tuples, NumPy arrays kept as arrays). `fig.data` is a tuple: add traces with `add_trace`, and assign to `fig.data` only to reorder or drop existing traces.
- `fig.batch_update()` (a context manager) groups many property changes into one update message, important for `FigureWidget` performance.
- Axis types are inferred from data: strings become `"category"`, date-like strings become `"date"`. Numeric-looking strings such as "2024" may be treated as numbers; set `type="category"` explicitly.
- `uirevision` in layout keeps the user's zoom and legend state when an app re-renders the figure.

`help(go.Scatter.marker)` or the reference pages document every attribute.
concepts.code:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px
from plotly.offline import get_plotlyjs_version

print(get_plotlyjs_version())                  # 4.x for Plotly 7

fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=["2024", "2025", "2026"], y=[3, 5, 4]))
print(fig.layout.xaxis.range)                  # None: filled in by plotly.js
fig.update_xaxes(type="category")              # don't let "2024" be a number

print(type(fig.data).__name__)                 # tuple
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=["2024", "2026"], y=[3, 4]))
fig.data = fig.data[::-1]                      # only reorder/drop allowed
print([t.type for t in fig.data])              # ['scatter', 'bar']

with fig.batch_update():                       # one message for widgets
    fig.data[1].marker.color = "#3F4F75"
    fig.layout.title.text = "Batched"

fig.update_layout(uirevision="keep")           # keep zoom across app re-renders
print(fig.to_plotly_json()["layout"]["uirevision"])  # keep
# full = fig.full_figure_for_development()     # needs kaleido + Chrome
takeaways: Python classes are generated from the plotly.js schema; versions are pinned together
plotly.js fills in defaults; `full_figure_for_development()` shows the resolved figure
Set axis `type` explicitly when data could be misread; use `uirevision` in apps
pitfalls: Reading `fig.layout.xaxis.range` to get the displayed range; it is None unless you set it.

quiz.q: Your x values are the strings '1', '2', '10' meant as labels, but the axis treats them as numbers. What fixes it?
quiz.explain: Plotly infers numeric axes from numeric-looking strings; an explicit category type keeps them as labels.

concepts.name: Reusable chart builders and testing figures
concepts.summary: Structure plotting code as pure functions that return figures, and test them by asserting on the figure's data and layout.
concepts.why: Charts in products and pipelines break silently; because Plotly figures are data, you can unit-test them like any other output.
concepts.code:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import pandas as pd

def revenue_chart(df: pd.DataFrame, target: float) -> go.Figure:
    df = df.sort_values("month")
    fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=df["month"], y=df["revenue"], name="revenue"))
    fig.add_hline(y=target, line_dash="dash")
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Revenue ($)", tickformat=",.0f")
    return fig

def test_revenue_chart():
    df = pd.DataFrame({"month": ["2026-02", "2026-01"], "revenue": [12, 10]})
    fig = revenue_chart(df, target=11)
    assert [t.type for t in fig.data] == ["bar"]
    assert list(fig.data[0].x) == ["2026-01", "2026-02"]   # sorted
    assert fig.layout.shapes[0].y0 == 11
    assert fig.layout.yaxis.title.text == "Revenue ($)"

test_revenue_chart()
print("ok")                                    # ok
takeaways: Write chart builders as pure functions returning a Figure
Test the figure's data and layout with targeted assertions
Make output deterministic and keep visual styling in templates
pitfalls: Snapshotting the entire figure JSON, which breaks on every plotly upgrade even when the chart is unchanged.

quiz.q: Why are targeted assertions preferred over comparing complete figure JSON?
options: Library upgrades change defaults and structure, breaking full snapshots without real regressions
quiz.explain: Only the parts you own should be locked down; full snapshots fail on unrelated library changes.
